attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his Substack essay, written in his own voice.

semantics.note: The draft says Deep Research is a fancier remake of Galactica and that, like it, Deep Research can write science-sounding articles on any topic on demand. That matches the statement. 'Essentially' adds a little, but the sarcastic framing does not change the testable capability claim.

contract.note: The contract reads 'remake' as a functional analogy and 'any topic' as broad topical choice. That is the fair, ordinary reading of firm language. A literal no-restrictions reading would stretch the words against the speaker.

evidence.note: OpenAI's launch page from 2025-02-02. It describes prompted reports with citations across science, finance, policy and consumer topics. This is the company describing its own product, but it does show what the product does.
The Galactica paper from November 2022. It describes generating literature reviews and encyclopedia articles, which shows the scientific-writing function.

Independent reporting from 2022-11-18. Users got Galactica to write wiki articles on topics as varied as space bears and proteins. Its content-filter refusals on some topics (racism, AIDS) rule out only a literal 'every topic' reading.

reviews.rationale: On the fair broad-topic reading, launch-era sources show both systems produced research-style prose on topics users chose. Galactica's filter gaps (e3) narrow only a literal reading. The Deep Research evidence is OpenAI's own launch page, but it documents product function, which is what the contract asks for. The 'remake' analogy holds in functional terms.

attribution.note: Marcus's own closing line in his Substack essay.

semantics.note: 'When — not if' states the flood as certain, so this is an unqualified forecast with no deadline, not a conditional. The draft keeps both the flood and the 'trouble' consequence.

contract.note: The ordinary reading (a large influx of unreliable medical content traceable to Deep Research, causing substantial problems) is fair. The contract also correctly says that no influx so far cannot refute a forecast with no deadline.

evidence.note: A 2026 preprint on citation URL failures, including Deep Research's rate of hallucinated URLs on a general benchmark. It does not measure medical content spreading at scale or any harm.
A small 2026 study in which Deep Research-assisted answers to knee-arthroplasty questions scored well. It neither shows nor rules out an influx of bad medical content or downstream harm.

reviews.rationale: This is a firm forecast with no deadline. The early-resolution rule for support has not been met: no audit establishes a widespread influx of unreliable medical content attributable to Deep Research, or harm resulting from one. No decisive event rules the forecast out either. The two studies are only context, so the claim stays unresolved.
